analysis.one_liner: Protects family farmers from big meatpackers through antitrust enforcement and payment guarantees.
analysis.headline: A bill to shield family farms from anticompetitive meatpackers was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new Justice Department office dedicated to agriculture antitrust cases, given the Agriculture Secretary a formal role reviewing large meatpacking and agribusiness mergers, required livestock dealers to hold proceeds in trust until sellers were paid, and set up a fund to compensate producers harmed by packers' anticompetitive conduct. It also would have voided contract clauses that gag farmers from sharing contract terms with lawyers or lenders, and added enforcement staff to police the meatpacking industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers who sell livestock, poultry, and grain to a shrinking set of large buyers. They would gain a guaranteed path to payment when a dealer's check bounces, a public record of how mergers would affect the prices they are paid, enforcement resources aimed at meatpacker concentration, and the legal right to share their contract terms when seeking advice.

how_it_helps.text: Livestock dealers would have to hold the proceeds and inventory from cash sales in trust for unpaid sellers until full payment, with civil damages and fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation for dealers who fail to do so.

The Agriculture Secretary would review mergers over $50 million involving livestock or commodity buyers and organic-input manufacturers, publish the notices for public comment, and report on effects on the prices paid to producers, regionally and nationally.

A new Senate-confirmed Assistant Attorney General for Agriculture Competition would oversee agriculture antitrust matters, with new staffing funded for 2001-2003, and the Grain Inspection, Packers and Stockyards Administration would get litigating attorneys to monitor meatpacking.

Confidentiality clauses in livestock and grain production contracts would be unenforceable when they bar a farmer from sharing contract terms to get legal or financial advice, and half of the fines and settlements from packer antitrust enforcement would go into a fund compensating harmed producers.

analysis.who_pays: Large livestock dealers and market agencies, who would bear trust obligations, fines, and damages; big meatpackers and agribusiness buyers, who would face merger scrutiny, added enforcement staffing, and a compensation fund paid from their antitrust penalties; and taxpayers, who would fund the new Justice Department office and additional inspectors.

drawbacks.text: The dealer trust rule would raise financing costs for livestock dealers, since lenders would lose their priority claim over inventories and receivables from cash-bought livestock, and those costs could be passed back to sellers in the prices offered.

The bill adds new layers of review and spending: a Senate-confirmed Justice Department position, open-ended appropriations for 2001-2003, merger reviews with mandatory public comment periods that could delay deals, and fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation, with an exemption only for small dealers averaging under $250,000 in annual purchases.

Small family-scale dealers were exempted below $250,000 in annual purchases, so the compliance burden falls mainly on mid-size and large dealers, some of whom are themselves regional businesses rather than national packers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For family farmers, the protections are concrete and targeted: payment security, merger transparency, contract-reading rights, and enforcement resources. The costs fall mostly on larger dealers and packers in the form of financing costs, fines, and regulatory review, with a modest taxpayer cost for staffing. The bill is narrower than full structural reform of meatpacking concentration, but the burden it creates is one its backers would argue is the point of antitrust law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out for a vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Ashcroft introduced the Fair Play for Family Farms Act of 2000 on June 15, 2000, with introductory remarks in the Senate.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, which was the last action of any kind recorded.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The bill text contained no floor votes, no committee markup, and no further action through the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large livestock dealers and meatpacking companies, who faced no new trust requirements, merger review, or compensation fund. Family farmers remained without the payment guarantees and enforcement resources the bill offered.

for.name: Sen. John Ashcroft
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 15, 2000 and took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to show a partisan split; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected their mergers to Agriculture Department review with public comment, funded a dedicated antitrust prosecutor, and diverted half of their antitrust fines and settlements into a fund paying the producers they harmed. Their gain under the status quo is concentrated buying power over farmers.

They would have had to hold cash-sale proceeds and inventories in trust for unpaid sellers, exposing lenders' collateral claims and adding fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation and full damages; dealers averaging under $250,000 in annual purchases were exempt.

industries.industry: Family farmers and ranchers (livestock, poultry, grain producers)
industries.note: Producers selling into concentrated markets would gain guaranteed payment through the dealer trust, the right to show contract terms to lawyers and lenders, merger transparency, and a compensation fund for antitrust harms.

industries.industry: Agricultural input manufacturers (organic inputs, seeds, chemicals)
industries.note: Mergers over $50 million involving organic agricultural input makers would face the same Agriculture Secretary review and public comment as livestock buyers, adding scrutiny and delay for large deals while leaving the industry otherwise untouched.
